tools.description: Run a command line in this conversation's own hidden zsh. The shell lives as long as the conversation: cd, exported variables and aliases carry over between calls, and it has the user's environment and startup files. It starts in the user's working directory. The answer has the output, the exit code and the directory after the command. A command still running at the timeout keeps running: when it waits for input (a sudo password, a [Y/n] question) the user can answer on the shell's screen, and the next call waits for it to end. Set nested_shell when the command must go to a shell you started inside this one, such as sudo -i or ssh.

command.description:
The command line, as you would type it at a zsh prompt. It may span several
lines.

nested_shell.description:
True to type the command into a shell that runs inside the hidden one (one you
started with `sudo -i`, `bash` or `ssh`), which has no efr integration.

timeout_seconds.description:
How many seconds to wait for the command to end before answering with what is
known; the command keeps running after that. Default 30, at most 600.

tools.name: shell

tools.description: Read a text file. Relative paths start at the user's working directory; ~ is the home directory. Use offset and limit to read a range of lines of a long file. A path through a symbolic link fails and names the real path.

limit.description: How many lines to show. Default: every line to the end.

offset.description: The first line to show, counted from 1. Default: 1.

path.description:
The file to read: absolute, relative to the user's working directory, or under
`~`.

tools.name: read_file

tools.description: Write the whole content of a text file, creating it and its parent directories when they are missing. Relative paths start at the user's working directory; ~ is the home directory. The original is kept so the change can be undone. A path through a symbolic link fails and names the real path.

content.description: The whole new content of the file.

path.description:
The file to write: absolute, relative to the user's working directory, or under
`~`. Missing parent directories are created.

tools.name: write_file
